description: Queremos formar algo grande a partir de pasos pequeños
summary:
Germina Finance is a decision-support platform created by team Respawn Earth for the NASA Space Apps crop rotation challenge. It is designed for small rural farmers in northern Cartago, Costa Rica, where monoculture, heavy rains and erosion on steep slopes wear down the soil and make incomes unstable.

The platform combines NASA Earth observations (weather, rainfall, soil moisture, slope and vegetation health) with local data and each farmer’s priorities. With this information, it compares the current rotation with other alternatives and explains in plain language why each one makes sense. It also shows the evidence, benefits, risks, confidence level and information gaps behind every suggestion. Recommendations are estimates, never guarantees.

In addition, it integrates basic finances: the minimum selling price to avoid a loss, profit per crop and a harvest history. This way, every environmental recommendation also makes economic sense for the family that depends on the farm.

The app is designed for people with little technological experience or low literacy. It uses clear icons, traffic-light alerts, read-aloud, adjustable text size, high-contrast modes and works without an internet connection.

Germina suggests; the farmer decides, with support from local technicians at MAG and INTA, Costa Rica’s agricultural agencies.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Germina Finance is a decision-support platform for small farmers in northern Cartago, Costa Rica. It helps them plan crop rotations that protect the soil and keep income stable. It combines four kinds of information:

NASA Earth observations: weather and rainfall (NASA POWER, GPM), soil moisture (SMAP), slope (SRTM) and vegetation health (MODIS).

Local soil data (SoilGrids) and weather forecasts (Open-Meteo).

Each farmer’s own records.

The farmer’s priorities, such as saving water, cutting erosion or increasing income.

With this, the platform compares the farmer’s current rotation with alternatives and ranks them by those priorities. For each option it explains, in plain language, why it is suggested, the evidence behind it, its benefits and risks, the gaps in the information, and how confident the suggestion is. It also includes basic farm finances: the minimum selling price to avoid a loss, profit per crop and a harvest history. Alerts use a traffic-light system to warn about heavy rain, market oversupply or fire hotspots.

What benefits does it have?

Turns complex satellite data into simple, practical advice.

Lowers the risk of soil erosion, nutrient depletion and pest cycles caused by monoculture.

Links environmental choices to their economic results, so sustainable practices also make financial sense.

Works offline and is accessible to people with little technical experience or low literacy.

What is the intended impact?

We want rotation decisions based on evidence to be available to farmers who are usually left out of digital agriculture tools. Over time, this should lead to healthier soil, less erosion on steep plots, better use of water and steadier incomes for rural families. Germina supports farmer judgment and never replaces it. Every suggestion is meant to be reviewed with local technicians from MAG and INTA.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

Design system and prototype: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (React components), with design tokens for color, type and spacing.

Accessibility checks: WCAG contrast checks and a palette validated for color blindness.

Videos: three.js for the 3D animation, Playwright and Chrome for screen capture, and FFmpeg for editing.

AI assistance: we used Claude (Anthropic) for design, prototyping, translation, video production, reviewing our documents for contradictions and gaps, and digitizing diagrams. This is described in our AI use statement.

Data sources planned: the NASA datasets listed above, plus SoilGrids and Open-Meteo.

Target hardware: low-cost Android phones and web browsers.

How is the project creative?

Rotations explained, not just ranked: most tools recommend a single crop. Germina compares whole rotations side by side, shows when the soil is left bare and is open about uncertainty.

Environment and finance together: soil health and farm finances live in one place.

Built for low literacy:

icon-first screens with no emojis;

traffic-light alerts that use color, icon and label together;

read-aloud on every screen;

text sizes from 100% to 175%;

day, night and high-contrast themes;

every color can be adjusted.

What factors did the team consider?

Users: limited digital experience, low literacy, older adults and children who help on the farm.

Connectivity: rural internet is unreliable, so the app works offline and syncs later.

Local context: steep slopes, intense rainy seasons and crops typical of the area, such as potato, onion and cabbage.

Trust and ethics: honest confidence levels, a clear “estimate, not a guarantee” message, data privacy and human review of every suggestion.

Feasibility: free, open data sources and a design that runs on inexpensive phones.
